items.title: Stratified sampling deliberately includes defined subgroups
items.claim: Why use stratified sampling rather than random?

options.text: Stratified sampling deliberately includes proportions from defined subgroups (e.g. age categories in a questionnaire, river sections by gradient), reducing the risk of missing minority categories

items.reveal:
Sampling types: random (every member equally likely), systematic (every nth member — e.g. every 10 m along a river transect), stratified (proportional samples from defined groups), opportunistic (whoever is available — least rigorous).

GCSE and A-level NEA fieldwork requires explicit justification of sampling strategy. Small samples (n<30) limit statistical analysis; subgroup analysis needs larger samples in each stratum.

Fieldwork ethics — informed consent for questionnaires, minimising impact on study sites — has become more prominent in awarding-body specifications.
items.why: Bad sampling produces bad results regardless of subsequent analysis. Sampling design is upstream of every statistical inference — and is the most common point of failure in student fieldwork.

items.title: Rural-urban migration is mostly young adults
items.claim: Who migrates from rural areas to cities in low- and middle-income countries?

options.text: Whole families move together as a single unit

Predominantly young adults (15-35) seeking employment, with selective patterns by gender — some societies see male-dominated industrial migration, others (e.g. textiles in Bangladesh, domestic work in the Philippines) see female-dominated
Elderly people seek better healthcare in cities
Migration is randomly distributed across all age groups

items.reveal:
Selective migration reshapes both source (ageing populations, women-headed households where men migrate, remittance economies) and destination (skewed urban demographics, housing pressure).

Mexico-US migration is largely male; Filipina overseas workers are mostly women. Bangladesh garment-industry urban migration is around 80% female. Pacific Island remittance dependence is heavy.

Remittances to LICs and MICs reached around $640 billion in 2022 (World Bank) — more than total foreign direct investment to many countries.
items.why: Migration is age- and gender-selective in ways that reshape entire economies. Treating migration as a uniform mass misses the demographic specifics that drive both impacts and policy.

items.title: Cities are 2-10 °C warmer than surrounding countryside
items.claim: What is the urban heat island (UHI) effect?

options.text: A myth — cities are no warmer than rural areas
Cities are typically 2-5 °C warmer than surrounding rural areas (up to 10 °C in extreme cases at night) due to dark surfaces, reduced evapotranspiration, anthropogenic heat and reduced sky view
Cities are colder than countryside due to shade
Only New York shows the effect

items.reveal:
Causes of UHI: dark asphalt and concrete have low albedo (absorb solar radiation); reduced vegetation cuts evaporative cooling; tall buildings trap re-emitted infrared (sky-view factor); waste heat from vehicles and air conditioning; thermal mass releases heat at night.

London during the 2003 heatwave was around 4-9 °C warmer than surrounding countryside at night. UHI contributed to the death toll (around 2,000 excess deaths in the UK).

Mitigation: green roofs, urban trees, light-coloured surfaces, water features, ventilation corridors in city planning.
items.why: Urban climate is human-made microclimate. Climate change interacts with UHI to make heatwaves more dangerous in cities — a fast-rising public health hazard.
